newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION - PARTIES' POSITIONS ON EMU.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION - PARTIES' POSITIONS ON EMU.

text.p: France will hold an early two-stage parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1. One of the key issues is European economic and monetary union (EMU) and the creation of a single currency on January 1, 1999.
The Maastricht treaty set several criteria for joining the euro, of which the key one is limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
Here is a summary of the main parties' positions on EMU:
RALLY FOR THE REPUBLIC (GAULLIST)
The senior partner in the ruling conservative coalition, founded by President Jacques Chirac and led by Prime Minister Alain Juppe, is firmly committed to launching the euro on time.
One of the reasons Chirac gave for his early election call was to allow France to accelerate and deepen European integration from a position of strength.

Government ministers have repeatedly pledged to do whatever is needed to keep deficits under three percent. They say adhering to the criteria will boost the economy's health and make the euro as strong and trustworthy as the dollar and the yen.

"France has nothing to fear but everything to gain from the euro, everything to gain from the Union and everything to gain from Europe," Juppe said in a speech on April 22. "(We need) the euro now, because afterwards it will be too late."
UNION FOR FRENCH DEMOCRACY (CENTRIST)
The UDF, junior partner in the ruling coalition, says achieving the single currency on time is "a fundamental, non-negotiable objective".
It says the euro is indispensable to create monetary stability that would attract investment to Europe and favour economic growth and employment.
The UDF platform also called for "the creation of a hard core of (EU) states which favour closer integration, led by France and Germany".
SOCIALIST PARTY

The Socialists negotiated the Maastricht treaty and until recently were publicly committed to starting the euro according to its provisions. The late president Francois Mitterrand was one of the architects of the treaty.
The Socialists have recently tempered their support, saying they want the euro "but with conditions".
The party says creation of a single currency from 1999 is a political decision that should not be conditional on a dogmatic application of the criteria.
It says neither France nor Germany will meet all the criteria and a Socialist government would seek to renegotiate the criteria, if necessary, with its partners.

On April 20, Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin said that if the Socialists won the elections they would not agree to imposing a new round of budget austerity if that were needed to respect the Maastricht deficit criterion.

"If to respect the criteria of three percent, which Germany will probably not respect, if to do that we have to impose, with the jobless rate we have...a new cure of austerity on the country my answer is no. No to the absolute respect of the three percent criterion," he said in a television interview.
The party has laid down four conditions for taking part in a single currency:
-- the entry from the start of Italy and Spain, and Britain if it wants, to avoid creating a currency dominated by the German mark.
-- the creation of an "economic government", a political counterweight to offset the power of a European central bank.
-- the creation of an EU pact of solidarity and growth to help create jobs.
-- that the euro should not be overvalued compared to the dollar.
COMMUNIST PARTY
The Communists have demanded for a fresh referendum on the single currency, calling the creation of the euro an "ultra-liberal political project".

"I am fundamentally in favour of the construction of Europe. But I think we should have a common currency, which implies the the preservation of a national currency, rather than a single currency," party leader Rober Hue has said.
NATIONAL FRONT
The extreme-right party is militantly opposed to the single currency and if it controlled parliament it would halt progress toward further European integration of most kinds.
It backs the idea of a fresh referendum on the euro.
GREENS

Like the Socialists, the Greens have said they are in favour of a single currency but with conditions. A party document published in early April says creation of the euro must "condition the objective of the single currency on a common political, economic and social project which turns its back on liberalism and deregulation and promotes lasting development".

The party also wants to scrap the existing stability pact, which is meant to ensure EU countries do not run up big deficits after the euro starts, and substitute for it a "solidarity and lasting development" pact based on policies to promote jobs creation, social progress and environmental protection.
The Greens broadly support further European integration.
